descriptions: satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma — truth, knowledge, infinite (TU 2.1.1)
sad eva ... ekam evādvitīyam — being alone, one without a second (ChU 6.2.1)
vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma — understanding, bliss (BAU 3.9.28); raso vai saḥ (TU 2.7.1)
that from which beings are born, by which they live, into which they enter (TU 3.1.1)
sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma — all this is brahman (ChU 3.14.1); brahmaivedaṃ viśvam (MuU 2.2.11)
pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam — that is full, this is full (BAU 5.1.1)
the Lord who wields māyā, whose power is innate knowledge and strength (ŚU 4.10, 6.8)
negations: asthūlam anaṇu ... — not gross, not fine ... without inside or outside (BAU 3.8.8)
aśabdam asparśam arūpam avyayam (KU 1.3.15); adreśyam agrāhyam (MuU 1.1.6)
yato vāco nivartante — from which words turn back with the mind (TU 2.4.1)
known by the one to whom it is unknown (Kena 2.3)
relation_to_self: The self is declared to be brahman (ahaṃ brahmāsmi, tat tvam asi, ayam ātmā brahma, prajñānaṃ brahma); it is also the inner controller of every being (BAU 3.7) and, in the two-birds image, the Lord beside the grieving self (MuU 3.1.1-2; ŚU 4.6-7).
relation_to_world: The source, support and end of all beings (TU 3.1.1); the world is woven on the imperishable (BAU 3.8) and pervaded by the Lord (Īśa 1); it emanates like sparks from fire (BAU 2.1.20; MuU 2.1.1), becomes manifest by name and form (BAU 1.4.7; ChU 6.3.2), and its modifications are 'a verbal handle, a name' (ChU 6.1.4); in the ŚU the māyin projects it by māyā-prakṛti (4.9-10).
caveat: The Upaniṣads do not systematize; they state identity (the mahāvākyas), difference (the two birds; the inner controller 'other than' what it controls) and a personal Lord (Śvetāśvatara). The later Vedānta schools read these same texts in very different ways — see dsp:tat-tvam-asi, dsp:souls-one-or-distinct, dsp:world-real-or-appearance, dsp:saguna-nirguna and dsp:being-or-non-being-first; this view records the statements without deciding between those readings.
